questions.question: A heart cell and a skin cell hold the same DNA. Which best explains why they behave so differently?
options: Each one deleted the recipes it does not need, keeping only its own.
Each one reads the same genes, but in a different order.
Each uses a different set of genes, switched on while the rest stay closed.
Each one received a different copy of the book when the egg divided.
questions.correct_answer: Each uses a different set of genes, switched on while the rest stay closed.
questions.why: Nearly every cell keeps the whole book. What differs is which pages are open.

questions.question: Which is the correct order of the path from recipe to worker?
options: DNA is copied into RNA, and the RNA is read to make a protein.
DNA is read to make a protein, and the protein is copied into RNA.
RNA is copied into DNA, and the DNA is read to make a protein.
RNA is read to make DNA, and the DNA folds into a protein.
questions.correct_answer: DNA is copied into RNA, and the RNA is read to make a protein.

questions.question: Fingers start out joined as a paddle. What frees them?
options: Cells between the fingers stretch until the fingers pull apart.
Cells between the fingers die on schedule.
Extra cells grow between the fingers and push them apart.
Cells between the fingers turn into bone and separate the fingers.
questions.correct_answer: Cells between the fingers die on schedule.
questions.why: Making way is part of building shape, like a sculptor taking clay away.

questions.question: What happens to the book just before a cell divides?
options: The book is split in half, so each new cell gets half.
Only the recipes the new cells will need are copied.
A working RNA copy of every recipe is made and handed over in place of the book.
The whole book is copied, so each new cell gets a full set.
questions.correct_answer: The whole book is copied, so each new cell gets a full set.
questions.why: Each new cell needs the whole book.

questions.question: Why does a signal that gets weaker with distance help a growing embryo?
options: Each cell can read how strong the signal is, and so sense roughly where it stands.
Cells close to the source copy their DNA faster than far ones.
Only the nearest cell responds, and it tells the others what to do.
Cells that receive a weak signal switch off all of their genes.
questions.correct_answer: Each cell can read how strong the signal is, and so sense roughly where it stands.
questions.why: A smooth change in strength sorts identical cells into different jobs by position.

questions.question: Which description of the path from one gene to a working protein fits the library and kitchen picture?
options: The original book leaves the library and is read in the kitchen, then folds into a protein.
A working RNA copy of just that recipe leaves the library. A cook reads it three letters at a time, links the ingredients into a chain, and the chain folds into a shape that does the job.
A complete copy of the whole book is sent to the kitchen, and the cook copies it back into DNA.
The cook goes into the library, reads the original book there, and carries the finished protein back out.
questions.correct_answer: A working RNA copy of just that recipe leaves the library. A cook reads it three letters at a time, links the ingredients into a chain, and the chain folds into a shape that does the job.
questions.why: The original book stays in the library, the nucleus. A temporary RNA copy of just that recipe goes to the kitchen. A ribosome reads it three letters at a time, builds a chain, and the chain folds into a shape that does the job.

questions.question: What is a gene?
options: One of the four chemical letters that DNA is written in.
A stretch of DNA that holds one useful instruction, like one recipe.
A full copy of the book, kept in one cell.
A protein that reads the book and carries it out of the nucleus.
questions.correct_answer: A stretch of DNA that holds one useful instruction, like one recipe.
questions.why: Letters make the recipes, recipes make the book.

questions.question: Some genes act like foremen on a building site. Which description fits them best?
options: They hold a detailed picture of each body part and hand it to the cells.
They do the building themselves, as proteins that become the part.
They are switches active in one stretch of the body, setting off whole sets of other genes that build the right kind of part there.
They switch on only after an injury, to rebuild what was lost.
questions.correct_answer: They are switches active in one stretch of the body, setting off whole sets of other genes that build the right kind of part there.

questions.question: What mostly decides what job a protein can do?
options: Which parent supplied the gene.
How fast the ribosome worked when it made the chain.
How many nuclei the cell has.
Its folded shape.
questions.why: Shape is everything: a key for one lock, a rope, an oxygen carrier.

questions.question: A skin cell divides, and both daughters are skin cells. What helps them stay that way?
options: The daughters keep only the skin recipes and discard the rest.
Chemical tags on the DNA, like bookmarks, are copied along and keep the same pages open.
The neighboring skin cells rewrite the DNA of each daughter.
The old RNA copies are handed to the daughters and reused.
questions.correct_answer: Chemical tags on the DNA, like bookmarks, are copied along and keep the same pages open.
questions.why: The book is still whole; the notes about which pages to use are passed along.

questions.question: A salamander can regrow a lost leg, with the right bones in the right places. Which split is correct?
options: Established: electrical patterns store the target shape in all animals. Open question: whether a salamander can regrow a lost leg.
Established: a salamander can regrow a lost leg with the right parts in the right places. That also settles how cells know the overall shape and when to stop.

Established: a salamander can regrow a lost leg with the right parts in the right places. Open question: how a group of cells knows the overall shape and when to stop. Levin's proposal, still being tested: electrical patterns across a tissue may act like a stored target shape.
Established: Levin has shown that electrical patterns are the stored target shape. Open question: whether genes play any part in building a leg.
questions.correct_answer: Established: a salamander can regrow a lost leg with the right parts in the right places. Open question: how a group of cells knows the overall shape and when to stop. Levin's proposal, still being tested: electrical patterns across a tissue may act like a stored target shape.
questions.why: The regrowth itself is well established. How a group of cells knows the overall shape and when to stop is still open. Levin's idea that electrical patterns may act like a stored target shape is a proposal, still being tested, not settled fact.

questions.question: Brothers and sisters resemble each other but are not identical. Which explanation is closest?
options: Each child gets half of its book from each parent, but a different mix.
Each child gets the whole book from just one parent, chosen differently.
Each child gets the same book, but the environment before birth changes the letters.
Each child gets the same book, but uses different pages at birth.
questions.correct_answer: Each child gets half of its book from each parent, but a different mix.
questions.why: Same two parent books, shuffled differently.

questions.question: Why does the original DNA stay in the nucleus when a gene is used?
options: The recipe is cut out of the book, carried out, and pasted back afterward.
A working copy of only that recipe is made, and the original stays safe.
A complete second copy of the book is made and carried out.
Ribosomes go into the nucleus, read the book there, and bring out the finished protein.
questions.correct_answer: A working copy of only that recipe is made, and the original stays safe.
questions.why: The original is precious, so a temporary copy goes to the kitchen.

questions.question: Which statement about Michael Levin's electrical idea is labeled correctly?
options: It is established: electrical patterns store the target shape of the body in all animals.
It is a proposal: genes play no part in shaping the body, and electricity does all of it.
It is a proposal: patterns of electrical signals across tissue may help guide body shape beyond genes, and it is still being tested.
It is established: electrical signals replace chemical signals once the body is formed.
questions.correct_answer: It is a proposal: patterns of electrical signals across tissue may help guide body shape beyond genes, and it is still being tested.
questions.why: It adds to genes and chemical signals; it does not replace them.

questions.question: Use the cookbook picture: how can two different cells hold the same book?
options: One cookbook can sit in a bakery and a pizzeria. Each kitchen opens only the pages it needs, so the same book yields different meals.
Each kitchen keeps only the pages it needs and tears the rest out, so the books are no longer the same.
The two kitchens have different cookbooks, printed with different recipes from the start.
Both kitchens open every page, but they cook the recipes in a different order, and that alone makes them different.
questions.correct_answer: One cookbook can sit in a bakery and a pizzeria. Each kitchen opens only the pages it needs, so the same book yields different meals.
questions.why: One cookbook can sit in a bakery and a pizzeria. Each kitchen opens only the pages it needs. The book is the same; the pattern of open pages differs, so the cells make different proteins.

questions.question: No single cell holds the plan of the whole body. How can a whole body in the right proportions still come about?
options: A master cell holds the full plan and tells every other cell exactly what to become.
Each cell follows a complete map of the finished body stored in its own DNA, so local clues are not needed.
Cells first grow as a uniform mass, then a later signal stamps the overall proportions onto the whole body at once.
Each cell follows local clues, such as the signals it receives and the neighbors it touches. Many small local actions add up to the overall pattern, a bit like a flock of birds turning together.
questions.correct_answer: Each cell follows local clues, such as the signals it receives and the neighbors it touches. Many small local actions add up to the overall pattern, a bit like a flock of birds turning together.
questions.why: No single cell holds the plan. Each cell follows local clues, and many small local actions add up to the overall pattern, a bit like a flock of birds turning together without a leader. Fading signals also give cells a sense of where they are.
